facts.fact: Newton, joule, watt and pascal are derived units, not base units.
Distance, speed, mass and energy are scalars (size only).
Displacement, velocity, acceleration and force are vectors (size and direction).
Newton's first law defines inertia.
Newton's second law gives F = ma.
Newton's third law: action and reaction are equal and opposite and act on different bodies.
Momentum = mass × velocity and is conserved in collisions.
The area under a velocity–time graph gives displacement.
Uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity.
g is greater at the poles (about 9.83) than at the equator (about 9.78).
g on the Moon is about one-sixth of its value on Earth.
Weight is zero at the centre of the Earth.
Acceleration due to gravity does not depend on the mass of the falling body.
One horsepower is about 746 watts.
Kinetic energy = ½mv²; potential energy = mgh.
Work is zero when the force is perpendicular to the displacement.
Archimedes' principle: upthrust equals the weight of fluid displaced.
A body floats when its density is less than that of the fluid.
A hydrometer measures the density of liquids and works on the principle of flotation.
Atmospheric pressure decreases with increasing altitude.
Pressure in a fluid P = hρg rises with depth.
Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.
A convex mirror (diverging, erect diminished image) is used as a rear-view mirror.
A concave mirror converges light (headlights, torches, shaving mirror).
A convex lens converges light (magnifying glass).
Splitting of white light into VIBGYOR by a prism is dispersion.
Sound needs a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum.
Sound travels fastest in solids and slowest in gases (about 343 m/s in air).
Human audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Ultrasound is above 20,000 Hz; infrasound below 20 Hz.
SONAR uses ultrasonic waves (echo) to measure sea depth.
Radiation is the only mode of heat transfer that works in a vacuum.
Sea and land breezes are examples of convection.
Water has a high specific heat, which moderates coastal climate.
Latent heat changes the state of a substance at constant temperature.
Ohm's law V = IR holds at constant temperature.
In a series circuit the same current flows through every component.
Household wiring is in parallel.
A fuse is connected in series in the live wire and works by the heating effect of current.
Electromagnetic induction (moving magnet near a coil induces current) is the basis of the generator.
Electric power P = VI = I²R; energy is billed in kilowatt-hours.
Fission (splitting a heavy nucleus) runs nuclear reactors and the atom bomb.
Fusion of hydrogen into helium powers the Sun.
Alpha particles are helium nuclei; beta = electrons; gamma = EM radiation.
Sublimation is direct change of solid to vapour (camphor, dry ice).
Air is a mixture; water is a compound.
Rusting of iron is a chemical change.
Atomic number = number of protons.
Mass number = protons + neutrons.
Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers.
The valency of carbon is 4.
pH below 7 is acidic, 7 neutral, above 7 basic.
Acid + base gives salt + water (neutralisation).
Baking soda is sodium hydrogen carbonate (NaHCO₃).
Washing soda is sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O).
Bleaching powder is calcium oxychloride (CaOCl₂).
Quicklime is calcium oxide; slaked lime is calcium hydroxide.
Plaster of Paris is calcium sulphate hemihydrate.
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.
Graphite is the non-metal that conducts electricity.
Filament bulbs are filled with argon or nitrogen to stop the filament oxidising.
Reactivity series: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag > Au.
Gold and silver are noble metals because of low reactivity.
Brass is copper + zinc.
Bronze is copper + tin.
Steel is iron + carbon; stainless steel adds chromium and nickel.
Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.
Methane (CH₄) is the simplest hydrocarbon.
Cellulose and natural rubber are natural polymers; polythene, PVC and nylon are synthetic.
Crops need N, P and K; urea is a nitrogenous fertiliser.
Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell.
Robert Brown discovered the cell nucleus.
A cell wall and chloroplasts are present in plant cells but absent in animal cells.
The neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system.
The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.
The medulla oblongata controls involuntary actions like heartbeat and breathing.
The liver is the largest gland; the pancreas is the second largest.
Gas exchange in the lungs takes place in the alveoli.
O-negative is the universal donor; AB is the universal recipient.
Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness.
Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.
Vitamin D deficiency causes rickets.
Vitamin B1 deficiency causes beriberi.
Iron deficiency causes anaemia; iodine deficiency causes goitre.
Insulin from the pancreas regulates blood glucose.
Thyroxine is secreted by the thyroid gland.
Adrenaline is the 'fight-or-flight' hormone.
The pituitary is the master gland at the base of the brain.
Photosynthesis uses chlorophyll and sunlight to make glucose from CO₂ and water.
Transpiration is loss of water vapour through leaf pores.
Whittaker's five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
metre (m) is the SI base unit of Length.
kilogram (kg) is the SI base unit of Mass.
second (s) is the SI base unit of Time.
ampere (A) is the SI base unit of Electric current.
kelvin (K) is the SI base unit of Thermodynamic temperature.
mole (mol) is the SI base unit of Amount of substance.
candela (cd) is the SI base unit of Luminous intensity.
The unit of Force is the newton (N).
The unit of Work and energy is the joule (J).
The unit of Power is the watt (W).
The unit of Pressure is the pascal (Pa).
The unit of Frequency is the hertz (Hz).
The unit of Electric charge is the coulomb (C).
The unit of Potential difference (voltage) is the volt (V).
The unit of Electrical resistance is the ohm (Ω).
The unit of Magnetic flux is the weber (Wb).
The unit of Magnetic field (flux density) is the tesla (T).
The unit of Capacitance is the farad (F).
The unit of Radioactivity is the becquerel (Bq).
The unit of Power of a lens is the dioptre (D).
The unit of Sound intensity level (loudness) is the decibel (dB).
The Light year measures or equals: distance travelled by light in one year (about 9.46 × 10^{12} km).
The Astronomical unit (AU) measures or equals: mean Earth–Sun distance (about 1.496 × 10^{8} km).
The Parsec measures or equals: about 3.26 light years (largest practical unit of distance).
The Angstrom measures or equals: 10^{-10} metre (used for wavelengths and atomic sizes).
The Nautical mile measures or equals: 1,852 metres (sea and air navigation).
The Knot measures or equals: speed of one nautical mile per hour (ships, aircraft).
The Fathom measures or equals: six feet — unit of depth of water.
The Kilowatt-hour (kWh) measures or equals: commercial unit of electrical energy = 3.6 × 10^{6} joules.
The Calorie measures or equals: heat needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C (about 4.18 joules).
The Mach number measures or equals: speed of a body divided by the speed of sound (above 1 = supersonic).
A Barometer measures atmospheric pressure.
A Hygrometer measures relative humidity of the air.
A Lactometer measures purity (density) of milk.
A Anemometer measures wind speed.
A Seismograph measures earthquake waves (intensity of earthquakes).
A Sphygmomanometer measures blood pressure.
A Ammeter measures electric current (connected in series).
A Voltmeter measures potential difference (connected in parallel).
A Galvanometer measures detects small electric currents.
A Odometer measures distance travelled by a vehicle.
A Altimeter measures altitude (height) of an aircraft.
A Pyrometer measures very high temperatures (furnaces).
A Fathometer measures depth of the sea (uses echo).
A Thermostat measures keeps a temperature constant automatically.
A Tachometer measures rotation speed of an engine shaft (rpm).
keys: rotation speed of an engine shaft

facts.fact: A Audiometer measures hearing ability (sound intensity).
A Manometer measures pressure of gases.
A Rain gauge (udometer) measures amount of rainfall.
A Stethoscope measures heart and lung sounds.
Same reading on Celsius and Fahrenheit: −40 degrees.
Absolute zero: 0 K = −273.15 °C.
Normal human body temperature: 37 °C = 98.6 °F.
Boiling point of water at sea level: 100 °C = 212 °F = 373 K.
Celsius to Fahrenheit: F = (9/5) × C + 32.
Pascal's law: pressure on an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions — hydraulic lift, press and brakes.
Bernoulli's principle: faster-moving fluid has lower pressure — lift on aeroplane wings, roofs blown off in storms.
Boyle's law: at constant temperature the volume of a gas varies inversely with its pressure.
Charles's law: at constant pressure the volume of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature.
Avogadro's law: equal volumes of gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.
Hooke's law: within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain — the spring balance.
Kepler's first law: planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus.
Newton's law of cooling: rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature difference with the surroundings.
Coulomb's law: force between two charges is proportional to their product and inversely to the square of the distance.
Joule's law of heating: heat produced H = I²Rt — basis of the electric heater, iron and fuse.
Lenz's law: an induced current always opposes the change that produced it.
Fleming's left-hand rule: direction of force on a current-carrying conductor — electric motor.
Fleming's right-hand rule: direction of induced current — electric generator.
Snell's law: law of refraction: sin i ÷ sin r is a constant (the refractive index).
Doppler effect: apparent change in frequency when source and observer move relative to each other — police speed radar, red shift of galaxies.
Tyndall effect: scattering of light by colloidal particles — a beam visible in a dusty room or misty forest.
Photoelectric effect: emission of electrons when light falls on a metal — explained by Einstein (Nobel Prize 1921); basis of solar cells.
Heisenberg's uncertainty principle: position and momentum of a particle cannot both be known exactly at the same time.
Passengers lurch forward when a bus brakes suddenly (seat belts needed) — explained by inertia of motion (Newton's first law).
Dust leaves a carpet when it is beaten — explained by inertia of rest.
A gun recoils when fired — explained by conservation of momentum (Newton's third law).
A rocket rises by throwing hot gases downward — explained by Newton's third law (action and reaction).
Raindrops are spherical; insects walk on water — explained by surface tension.
Oil rises up a lamp wick; blotting paper soaks ink — explained by capillarity (capillary action).
Honey flows more slowly than water — explained by viscosity (internal friction of a fluid).
Roads and railway tracks are banked at curves — explained by centripetal force needed for circular motion.
Escape velocity from Earth — explained by about 11.2 km per second.
Orbital velocity of a satellite close to Earth — explained by about 7.9 km per second.
Blue colour of the sky is caused by scattering of light (blue scattered most).
Red colour for danger signals is caused by red is scattered least (longest wavelength), so it is seen from far.
Reddish Sun at sunrise and sunset is caused by blue light scattered away over the long path through air.
Twinkling of stars is caused by atmospheric refraction.
Planets do not twinkle is caused by they are near and look like extended discs, not points.
Sun seen about 2 minutes before actual sunrise is caused by atmospheric refraction.
Mirage in deserts and on hot roads is caused by total internal reflection (with refraction) in hot air layers.
Sparkling of a diamond is caused by total internal reflection (very high refractive index of diamond).
Optical fibre carrying signals is caused by total internal reflection of light along the glass core.
Rainbow is caused by dispersion, refraction and internal reflection in raindrops (seen opposite the Sun).
Pool looks shallower; pencil looks bent in water is caused by refraction.
Speed of light in vacuum: about 3 × 10^{8} metres per second.
Time for sunlight to reach Earth: about 8 minutes 20 seconds.
Primary colours of light: red, green and blue.
Periscope: two plane mirrors (or prisms) at 45 degrees.
Kaleidoscope: multiple reflection between inclined plane mirrors.
Dentist's and shaving mirror; solar cooker: concave mirror.
Myopia (short-sightedness): far objects blurred; corrected with a concave lens.
Hypermetropia (long-sightedness): near objects blurred; corrected with a convex lens.
Presbyopia: age-related loss of focusing power; corrected with bifocal lenses.
Astigmatism: unequal curvature of the cornea; corrected with a cylindrical lens.
Cataract: eye lens becomes cloudy (opaque); treated by surgery.
Retina: light-sensitive screen where a real, inverted image forms.
Rods and cones: rods sense dim light; cones sense colour.
Iris: controls the size of the pupil.
Power of a lens: P = 1 ÷ focal length in metres; convex lens positive, concave negative.
Gamma rays: shortest wavelength, most penetrating; cancer treatment.
X-rays: imaging of bones; discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen (1895).
Ultraviolet rays: make vitamin D in skin, kill germs; mostly absorbed by the ozone layer.
Infrared rays: heat radiation; TV remote controls and night-vision devices.
Microwaves: radar and microwave ovens.
Radio waves: longest wavelength; radio and TV broadcasting.
Pitch (shrillness): depends on frequency — a woman's voice usually has higher pitch.
Loudness: depends on amplitude; measured in decibels.
Quality (timbre): depends on waveform — lets us tell instruments apart.
Speed of sound in water: about 1,500 metres per second (over four times faster than in air).
Speed of sound and temperature: speed of sound increases with temperature and humidity.
Echo: heard only if the reflector is at least about 17.2 m away (0.1 s gap).
Sound waves in air: longitudinal waves of compressions and rarefactions.
Bats and dolphins: use ultrasound to locate objects (echolocation).
Elephants and whales: communicate using infrasound.
Ultrasound in medicine: sonography of the foetus and organs; breaking kidney stones.
Sonic boom: shock wave when a body moves faster than sound (supersonic).
Reverberation: persistence of sound by repeated reflections in a large hall.
Water is densest at 4 °C — because of anomalous expansion — lakes freeze from the top and fish survive below.
Cooking is difficult at high altitude — because of lower air pressure lowers the boiling point of water.
A pressure cooker cooks faster — because of higher pressure raises the boiling point of water.
Water stays cool in an earthen pot (matka); sweating cools us — because of evaporation causes cooling.
Thermos (vacuum) flask — because of vacuum stops conduction and convection; silvered walls stop radiation.
Black surfaces get hot; white clothes are worn in summer — because of black is the best absorber and emitter of heat.
Gaps are left between railway rails — because of thermal expansion in summer.
Ice melts under pressure and refreezes (ice skating) — because of regelation — pressure lowers the melting point of ice.
Bimetallic strip in a thermostat — because of two metals expand unequally and the strip bends.
Household supply in India: AC at about 220–230 volts and 50 hertz.
Transformer: steps AC voltage up or down; works only on AC (mutual induction).
Heating element of heaters and irons: nichrome (nickel–chromium alloy).
Filament of an incandescent bulb: tungsten (melting point about 3,400 °C).
Fuse wire: alloy of tin and lead with a low melting point.
Best conductor of electricity: silver (copper is used in wiring as it is cheaper).
Semiconductors: silicon and germanium.
Colour code of house wires: live — red or brown; neutral — black or blue; earth — green.
LED lamp versus CFL: LED is more energy-efficient and has no mercury; a CFL contains mercury.
Diode: lets current flow one way — used as a rectifier (AC to DC).
Transistor: amplifier and electronic switch.
Electric cell (battery): chemical energy to electrical energy; gives DC (Volta made the first cell).
Solar (photovoltaic) cell: light energy to electrical energy; made of silicon.
Superconductor: zero electrical resistance at very low temperatures.
Resistance of a wire: increases with length and decreases with thickness (cross-section area).
Lightning conductor: pointed copper rod that leads charge to earth (Benjamin Franklin).
Hans Christian Oersted (1820): showed that an electric current produces a magnetic field.
Michael Faraday (1831): discovered electromagnetic induction (basis of the generator and transformer).
Core of an electromagnet: soft iron (magnetises and demagnetises easily).
Permanent magnets: steel or alloys such as alnico.
Earth as a magnet: Earth's geographic north is near its magnetic south pole, so a compass needle points north.
Magnetic poles: like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
Electron (1897) was discovered by J.J. Thomson.
Proton (canal rays, 1886) was discovered by E. Goldstein (named by Rutherford).
Neutron (1932) was discovered by James Chadwick.
Nucleus — gold-foil (alpha scattering) experiment, 1911 was discovered by Ernest Rutherford.
Electrons in fixed orbits (shells), 1913 was discovered by Niels Bohr.
Radioactivity (1896) was discovered by Henri Becquerel.
Polonium and radium was discovered by Marie and Pierre Curie.
X-rays (1895) was discovered by Wilhelm Röntgen — first Nobel Prize in Physics, 1901.
Mass–energy equivalence E = mc² was discovered by Albert Einstein.
Nuclear fission (1938) was discovered by Otto Hahn and Fritz Strassmann.
Penetrating power of radiations: gamma > beta > alpha (alpha is stopped by paper).
Half-life: time in which half the nuclei of a radioactive sample decay.
Carbon-14: radiocarbon dating of fossils and archaeological remains.
Cobalt-60: radiotherapy of cancer.
Iodine-131: diagnosis and treatment of thyroid disorders.
Uranium-235: fuel of nuclear fission reactors.
Heavy water (D₂O): moderator that slows neutrons in nuclear reactors.
Control rods: cadmium or boron rods that absorb neutrons.
Isotopes of hydrogen: protium, deuterium and tritium (tritium is radioactive).
Isobars: same mass number, different atomic numbers (argon-40 and calcium-40).
Mendeleev's periodic table (1869): elements arranged by atomic mass.
Modern periodic law (Moseley, 1913): elements arranged by atomic number.
Modern periodic table: 18 groups and 7 periods.
Number of known elements: 118.
Group 1: alkali metals (sodium, potassium).
Group 17: halogens (fluorine, chlorine, bromine, iodine).
Group 18: noble (inert) gases.
Döbereiner's triads and Newlands' law of octaves: early attempts at classifying elements.
Most abundant element in the Earth's crust: oxygen (silicon is second).
Most abundant metal in the Earth's crust: aluminium.
Most abundant gas in the atmosphere: nitrogen (about 78%; oxygen about 21%, argon about 0.93%).
Most abundant element in the universe: hydrogen.
Lightest element; lightest metal: hydrogen; lithium.
Only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature: bromine (mercury is the only liquid metal).
Most electronegative (most reactive non-metal): fluorine.
Metal that melts in the palm of the hand: gallium (melting point about 30 °C).
Helium is used for filling weather balloons and airships (light, non-inflammable); with oxygen in deep-sea diving cylinders.
Neon is used for glowing advertisement signs.
Argon is used for filling electric filament bulbs (with nitrogen).
Radon is used for radioactive noble gas used in radiotherapy.
Xenon is used for high-intensity lamps and camera flash tubes.
Vinegar contains acetic (ethanoic) acid.
Lemon and orange contains citric acid.
Tamarind (and grapes) contains tartaric acid.
Curd and sour milk contains lactic acid.
Ant sting and nettle sting contains formic (methanoic) acid.
Tomato contains oxalic acid.
Apple contains malic acid.
Gastric juice of the stomach contains hydrochloric acid.
Rancid butter contains butyric acid.
Car (lead-acid) battery contains sulphuric acid.
Soda water and soft drinks contains carbonic acid.
Litmus: natural indicator from lichens; acid turns blue litmus red, base turns red litmus blue.
Phenolphthalein: colourless in acid, pink in base.
Methyl orange: red in acid, yellow in base.
Turmeric: turns reddish-brown in a base (soap).
Milk of magnesia: magnesium hydroxide — an antacid.
Aqua regia: concentrated hydrochloric and nitric acids in a 3 : 1 ratio; dissolves gold and platinum.
Oil of vitriol ("king of chemicals"): sulphuric acid.
Tooth decay: starts when the pH in the mouth falls below about 5.5.
Acidic soil: treated with lime (quicklime or slaked lime).
Acid rain: rain with pH below about 5.6 (sulphur and nitrogen oxides).
Laughing gas: nitrous oxide (N₂O).
Dry ice: solid carbon dioxide.
Marsh gas: methane.
LPG (liquefied petroleum gas): mainly butane (with propane); ethyl mercaptan is added for smell.
CNG (compressed natural gas): mainly methane.
Biogas (gobar gas): mainly methane.
Bhopal gas tragedy (1984): methyl isocyanate (MIC).
Carbon monoxide: poisonous — binds haemoglobin to form carboxyhaemoglobin.
Gas in common fire extinguishers: carbon dioxide.
Caustic soda is sodium hydroxide (NaOH).
Blue vitriol is copper sulphate (CuSO₄·5H₂O).
Green vitriol is ferrous sulphate (FeSO₄·7H₂O).
Gypsum is calcium sulphate dihydrate (CaSO₄·2H₂O).
Limestone, marble and chalk is calcium carbonate (CaCO₃).
Sand (quartz) is silicon dioxide (SiO₂).
Potash alum (phitkari) is used to purify water (makes impurities settle).
Caustic potash is potassium hydroxide (KOH).
Bauxite is an ore of aluminium.
Haematite (and magnetite) is an ore of iron.
Cinnabar is an ore of mercury.
Galena is an ore of lead.
Zinc blende is an ore of zinc.
Chalcopyrite (copper pyrites) is an ore of copper.
Solder: lead + tin (joining wires).
German silver: copper + zinc + nickel — contains no silver.
Amalgam: mercury + another metal (dental fillings).
Duralumin: aluminium + copper (with magnesium, manganese) — aircraft bodies.
Gun metal: copper + tin + zinc.
Bell metal: copper + tin (more tin than bronze).
Magnalium: aluminium + magnesium.
22-carat gold: 22 parts gold + 2 parts copper or silver (24 carat = pure gold).
Rusting of iron: needs both oxygen (air) and water; rust is hydrated iron oxide.
Galvanisation: coating iron or steel with zinc.
Green coating on copper: basic copper carbonate.
Silver turns black: silver sulphide forms.
Sodium and potassium are stored in: kerosene (they react violently with air and water).
White phosphorus is stored in: water (it catches fire in air).
Temporary hardness of water: calcium and magnesium bicarbonates; removed by boiling.
Permanent hardness of water: chlorides and sulphates of calcium and magnesium; removed by washing soda or ion exchange.
Soap: sodium or potassium salt of fatty acids; forms scum in hard water (detergents do not).
Saponification: making soap from fat or oil and sodium hydroxide.
Disinfecting drinking water: chlorine or bleaching powder.
Teflon (PTFE): non-stick coating of cookware.
Nylon: first fully synthetic fibre (Wallace Carothers, 1935).
Bakelite: thermosetting plastic — electrical switches and handles.
Thermoplastics (polythene, PVC): soften on heating and can be remoulded.
Rayon: artificial silk made from cellulose (wood pulp).
Natural rubber: polymer of isoprene; hardened by vulcanisation with sulphur (Goodyear).
PET (polyethylene terephthalate): bottles and polyester fibre.
Fullerene (C₆₀, "buckyball"): football-shaped allotrope of carbon.
Methanol: poisonous alcohol — can cause blindness and death (spurious liquor).
Ethanol: alcohol of drinks; made by fermentation of sugar by yeast.
Octane number: measures anti-knocking quality of petrol (cetane number for diesel).
Law of conservation of mass: Antoine Lavoisier — mass is neither created nor destroyed in a reaction.
Law of definite (constant) proportions: Joseph Proust — a compound always has elements in a fixed mass ratio.
Atomic theory (1808): John Dalton.
Exothermic reactions: give out heat — burning of fuels and respiration.
Endothermic reactions: absorb energy — photosynthesis, dissolving ammonium chloride.
Oxidation and reduction: oxidation = gain of oxygen or loss of electrons; reduction is the reverse.
Catalyst: changes the rate of a reaction without being used up; enzymes are biological catalysts.
Artificial ripening of fruit: calcium carbide (releases acetylene) is banned; ethylene gas is the permitted ripener.
Nitrogen (N): leafy green growth (protein and chlorophyll).
Phosphorus (P): root development, flowering and seed formation.
Potassium (K): disease resistance and fruit quality.
Urea: about 46% nitrogen — the richest common nitrogen fertiliser.
DAP: diammonium phosphate — supplies nitrogen and phosphorus.
Cell first described (cork, 1665): Robert Hooke.
First to see living cells (bacteria, protozoa): Antonie van Leeuwenhoek.
Cell theory (1838–39): Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann.
"Every cell arises from a pre-existing cell": Rudolf Virchow.
Ribosomes: protein synthesis ("protein factories").
Lysosomes: "suicide bags" — digestive enzymes that break down waste.
Golgi apparatus: packaging and secretion of materials.
Endoplasmic reticulum: transport network; rough ER makes proteins, smooth ER makes lipids.
Centrosome (centrioles): found in animal cells; helps in cell division.
Mitochondria and chloroplasts: have their own DNA and ribosomes.
Prokaryotic cells (bacteria): no membrane-bound nucleus or organelles.
Largest single cell: egg of the ostrich.
Longest cell of the human body: nerve cell (neuron).
Smallest cell: Mycoplasma (PPLO).
Mitosis: division of body cells giving two identical daughter cells — growth and repair.
Meiosis: division that forms gametes and halves the chromosome number.
Chromosomes in a human body cell: 46 (23 pairs).
Sex of a child: decided by the father's sperm (X or Y chromosome); XX = girl, XY = boy.
Father of genetics: Gregor Mendel — experiments on the garden pea.
Double-helix model of DNA (1953): James Watson and Francis Crick.
Xylem: carries water and minerals up from the roots.
Phloem: carries food made in leaves to all parts (translocation).
Stomata: leaf pores for gas exchange and transpiration.
Oxygen released in photosynthesis: comes from the splitting of water (photolysis).
Auxin: cell elongation; bending of shoots towards light (phototropism).
Gibberellin: stem elongation and bolting; breaks seed dormancy.
Cytokinin: promotes cell division; delays ageing of leaves.
Abscisic acid: "stress hormone" — closes stomata and keeps seeds dormant.
Ethylene: gaseous hormone that ripens fruit.
Rhizobium: bacterium in root nodules of legumes that fixes atmospheric nitrogen.
Pitcher plant (Nepenthes): insectivorous plant (traps insects for nitrogen).
Cuscuta (dodder): parasitic plant without chlorophyll.
Binomial nomenclature (genus + species): Carl Linnaeus — father of taxonomy.
Five-kingdom classification (1969): R.H. Whittaker.
Father of biology (and of zoology): Aristotle.
Father of botany: Theophrastus.
Scientific name of humans: Homo sapiens.
Bones in an adult human: 206 (a newborn has about 300).
Longest bone: femur (thigh bone).
Smallest bone: stapes (stirrup) in the middle ear.
Largest organ of the body: skin.
Teeth in an adult: 32.
Hardest substance in the body: tooth enamel.
Normal blood pressure: 120/80 mm of mercury (systolic/diastolic).
Human heart: four chambers; beats about 72 times a minute at rest.
Circulation of blood discovered by: William Harvey (1628).
Blood volume of an adult: about 5–6 litres.
Red blood cells: carry oxygen using iron-rich haemoglobin; live about 120 days; made in bone marrow.
White blood cells: fight infection (immunity).
Platelets: help blood to clot.
Spleen: "graveyard of RBCs" — destroys old red cells.
ABO blood groups (1900): Karl Landsteiner.
Rh factor (1940): Landsteiner and Wiener — named after the rhesus monkey.
Plasma: liquid part of blood, about 55% of its volume.
Salivary amylase (ptyalin): begins digestion of starch in the mouth.
Pepsin (with hydrochloric acid): digests proteins in the stomach.
Bile: made by the liver, stored in the gall bladder; emulsifies fats (contains no enzyme).
Pancreatic juice: trypsin (proteins), lipase (fats) and amylase (starch).
Villi of the small intestine: absorb digested food (most absorption happens here).
Large intestine: absorbs water from undigested food.
Muscle cramps after hard exercise: lactic acid from anaerobic respiration.
Cerebrum: largest part of the brain — intelligence, memory, thinking, voluntary actions.
Cerebellum: balance and posture; coordination of movement.
Hypothalamus: controls body temperature, hunger and thirst.
Reflex actions: controlled by the spinal cord.
Islets of Langerhans (pancreas): insulin (lowers blood sugar) and glucagon (raises it).
Diabetes mellitus: too little insulin (or the body not responding to it).
Growth hormone (pituitary): excess in childhood causes gigantism; deficiency causes dwarfism.
Parathyroid gland: parathormone controls calcium level in blood.
Pineal gland: melatonin — sleep–wake cycle.
Thymus: maturation of T-lymphocytes (immunity); shrinks in adults.
Fat-soluble vitamins: A, D, E and K (B and C are water-soluble).
Vitamin D: made in the skin on exposure to sunlight; deficiency causes rickets.
Vitamin K: needed for clotting of blood.
Vitamin E: antioxidant; needed for fertility.
Vitamin B12: contains cobalt; deficiency causes pernicious anaemia.
Vitamin B3 (niacin): deficiency causes pellagra.
Chemical names of vitamins: A = retinol, B1 = thiamine, C = ascorbic acid, D = calciferol.
Vitamin C and cooking: vitamin C is destroyed easily by heat.
Kwashiorkor: protein deficiency in children (swollen belly).
Marasmus: deficiency of both protein and calories (wasting).
